title: Home & Everyday Life
description: Living in Indonesia: renting a kos, paying the bills, the water jug and the gas bottle, things that break and the people who fix them.

items.registerNotes: Signs say Terima Kos or Kost; kos putri and kos putra take only women or only men.
items.cultureNote: A kos is a room rented by the month, often with a shared bathroom. The landlady is the ibu kos, and the students and young workers who live there are anak kos.
A kontrakan is often rented by the year, with the whole year's rent paid in advance.

items.registerNotes: Sewanya berapa sebulan? (How much is the rent a month?) In speech sewa is also the verb, Saya sewa kamar di sini, where writing has menyewa.

items.pitfallNote: Tagihan is a bill for a service, like electricity, water or the internet. The bill at a warung or restaurant is the bon: Minta bonnya.

items.cultureNote: Many homes and kos rooms have a prepaid meter: you buy a token at a minimarket or in an app and type its code in. When the meter beeps, the credit is running out.
Tap water isn't for drinking, so homes buy drinking water by the galon, about 19 litres, for a dispenser. A local shop delivers a sealed one or a cheaper refill (isi ulang).

items.registerNotes: Gasnya habis (The gas has run out). The small green 3 kg bottle is called gas melon, after its shape and colour.
From the Dutch koelkast. Lemari es, literally ice cupboard, is the more formal word.

items.cultureNote: Many houses pump water from a well or the mains up to a tank, so when the power goes off, the water often stops too.

items.registerNotes: Mati lampu lagi (The power's out again). Literally the lights die; listrik mati means the same, and pemadaman listrik is the formal word in notices.

items.pitfallNote: Rusak is for machines and things that stop working: AC-nya rusak. A broken bone or stick is patah, and broken glass is pecah.

items.registerNotes: Atapnya bocor (The roof leaks), a classic rainy-season complaint. Ban bocor is a flat tyre.
Tukang plus the trade: tukang listrik (electrician), tukang ledeng (plumber), tukang AC. It also names street sellers and workers, like tukang sayur and tukang parkir.
items.cultureNote: Address a tukang as Pak or Mas, and offer a drink while he works; it's the norm.

items.registerNotes: Sedang dalam perbaikan on a sign means under repair. The verb is memperbaiki, literally to make good; in casual speech people say benerin.

items.cultureNote: Housing estates, offices and banks have a satpam at the gate, addressed as Pak. The word is short for satuan pengamanan.

Every neighbourhood is divided into small units called RT (rukun tetangga), each with a head chosen by the residents, Pak RT or Bu RT. Newcomers, foreigners included, are expected to report to them (lapor RT).

items.registerNotes: Jagalah kebersihan (Keep it clean) is on signs everywhere. Uang kebersihan is the monthly fee for rubbish collection, often collected through the RT.
The clothes being washed or waiting to be: Cucian saya belum kering (My washing isn't dry yet).
items.cultureNote: Many people send their washing to a laundry kiloan, paid by the kilo, which washes, dries and irons it.

items.english: to hang out to dry; to dry in the sun
items.registerNotes: In speech just jemur: Saya jemur baju dulu (I'll hang the washing out first). The washing on the line is the jemuran, and berjemur is to sunbathe.
As a verb it's menyetrika in writing and nyetrika or setrika in speech: Bajunya sudah disetrika? (Has the shirt been ironed?)
Shops and online listings usually spell it sprei. Ganti seprai is to change the sheets.

items.cultureNote: Most Indonesian beds also have a guling, a long bolster you hug while you sleep.

items.registerNotes: Obat nyamuk is mosquito repellent, whether a coil, a spray or a lotion. Mosquitoes spread dengue fever (demam berdarah), so people take them seriously.
